title: The Council of Nicaea: What Was Actually Decided in 325
excerpt: Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Jesus or pick the books of the Bible. What it actually did still decides what you believe about your own salvation.
body:
Most of what people think they know about the Council of Nicaea, they learned from a novel. The story, repeated until it feels like common knowledge, is that in the year 325 the emperor Constantine gathered the bishops, held a vote, and invented the divinity of Jesus, and that the same council decided which books would go in the Bible, the whole thing a political maneuver to consolidate imperial power. Almost every piece of that is false. What actually happened is harder, and more interesting, and it still decides things you believe about your own salvation.

## What Nicaea Did Not Do

Nicaea did not settle the canon of Scripture. No book was added or burned there. The legend that the council fixed the New Testament and suppressed the rejected gospels appears in no record of the proceedings, and even skeptical historians of early Christianity grant that the canon was simply not the council's business (Ehrman 2003). And Nicaea did not invent the divinity of Christ. Christians had been worshipping Jesus as Lord, singing to him as God, baptizing in his name, and dying rather than burn incense to Caesar for nearly three centuries before any emperor convened anything. You do not need a council to command you to worship someone you are already willing to be executed for refusing to deny.

## The Fight Over One Word

So what was the actual fight. A presbyter in Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son, though the first and highest of all beings, was a creature, made by the Father out of nothing before time began, so that, in his famous slogan, there was when the Son was not. The bishop Alexander and his young deacon Athanasius answered that the Son is eternally begotten, not made, of the same being as the Father. The entire conflict turned on one question. Is Jesus God in the full sense, or the greatest of God's creatures. The combatants fought over the same texts, John's claim that in the beginning the Word was with God and the Word was God (John 1:1 ESV), and Paul's that the Son is the firstborn of all creation, which Arius read as created and Athanasius read as heir and head over creation.

## Granting the Skeptic His Evidence

> Is Jesus God in the full sense, or the greatest of God's creatures.

Steel-man the skeptic, because the surface facts give him plenty to work with. Constantine did convene the council and did want unity in his fracturing empire. The politics were real and often sordid. The decisive term the council chose, homoousios, of the same being, was not found in the Bible, and its absence troubled even some who were no friends of Arius. And the controversy did not end at Nicaea. It raged for the rest of the century, and Athanasius was driven into exile five separate times, once under an emperor who had swung to the Arian side. A person looking only at the imperial machinery could be forgiven for mistaking the whole thing for politics.

But the substance was not invented, and the vote was not close. Of roughly three hundred bishops present, all but two signed the creed, and many of them carried in their own bodies the scars of the persecutions that had ended barely a decade earlier. These were not imperial functionaries. They were survivors of torture being asked by a brand-new and not-yet-baptized Christian emperor to settle a question the church had raised itself. They drew the line at of one being with the Father because they saw what Arius's tidy solution destroyed. Athanasius made the stakes plain. Only God can save. If the one on the cross is a creature, then a creature is our savior, and we are worshipping someone less than God, which is idolatry, and worse, a creature cannot join us to a God he is not (Athanasius 2011).

## The Reframe the Novel Misses

The modern historians have shown how far the old cynical story falls short. Lewis Ayres argues that Nicaea was a genuine stage in theological development, the church slowly working out the grammar of what it had always done in worship, not a foreign idea stamped onto simple faith by an emperor (Ayres 2004). Jaroslav Pelikan traced the same long development and showed that the creed did not break with the worship of the earlier church but defended it, naming in formal language the divine Christ the church had confessed from the beginning (Pelikan 1971). That is the reframe the novel misses entirely. The creed did not impose philosophy on a Galilean carpenter. It protected the carpenter, the plain confession that Jesus is Lord, from a sophisticated philosophical attempt to shrink him into a demigod.

## Why the Word Still Decides Your Salvation

> It protected the carpenter, the plain confession that Jesus is Lord, from a sophisticated philosophical attempt to shrink him into a demigod.

And it still matters, because a Christ who is merely the highest creature is a Christ who cannot save, and a Christianity built on him is a religion of admiring a fine example, which is to say a religion of works, you straining to follow a hero who cannot reach back. The entire weight of grace hangs on the one word the bishops fought for. If the one bleeding on the cross is God himself bearing what we owed, that is salvation. If he is a creature God dispatched to bear it, that is cosmic injustice with a halo. Everything you actually believe about whether you can be rescued is hiding inside that word.

## A Confession Signed in Blood

> If he is a creature God dispatched to bear it, that is cosmic injustice with a halo.

The bishops at Nicaea were not defending their power. Most of them had just finished losing everything for refusing to deny the very thing the council affirmed. They handed the church one word it could not read straight off the surface of the Bible but could not live without, and they were right to bleed for it. The novel got the drama right and the facts wrong. The truth was less of a conspiracy and more of a confession, signed by men who had already proven what their confession was worth.

### Works Cited

Athanasius. 2011. On the Incarnation. Translated by John Behr. Yonkers, NY: St Vladimir's Seminary Press.

Ayres, Lewis. 2004. Nicaea and Its Legacy. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Ehrman, Bart D. 2003. Lost Christianities. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

Pelikan, Jaroslav. 1971. The Christian Tradition, Volume 1. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.

title: How the Reformation Started and Why It Still Matters
excerpt: The Reformation was not mainly about corruption. It was about one question: how is a person made right with God. That question is still keeping you awake.
body:
Ask why the Reformation happened and you will usually hear about corruption. A monk named Martin Luther got angry that the church was selling indulgences, slips of paper promising to shorten a dead relative's time in purgatory, and he nailed his protest to a church door in Wittenberg in 1517, and the church split in two. That is true as far as it goes, and it does not go nearly far enough to explain why anyone was willing to die. People do not burn at the stake over administrative corruption. They burn over a question, and the question underneath the Reformation is the same one still keeping you awake at night.

## The Question Underneath the Corruption

The question is this. How is a person made right with God. Not how is the church funded, not who answers to whom, but the older and more personal terror. When I stand before God, on what basis am I accepted. Luther was an Augustinian monk doing everything the system prescribed, confessing for hours until he wore out his confessor, punishing his body, climbing the holy stairs in Rome on his knees, and he could find no peace, because he knew the standard was perfection and he knew he was not perfect, and a holy God could only condemn what was not.

## The Sentence That Broke Luther Open

Then he read Romans, and one sentence broke him open. The righteousness of God is revealed, Paul wrote, from faith for faith, as it is written, the righteous shall live by faith (Romans 1:17 ESV). Luther had always read the phrase the righteousness of God as a threat, the perfect standard that damned him. Now he saw it the other way. The righteousness in the verse is not the standard God demands but the gift God gives, a righteousness from outside us, the very righteousness of Christ credited to everyone who trusts him. He called that discovery the gate to paradise. Alister McGrath, tracing the long history of how the church has understood justification, locates Luther's breakthrough precisely in this turn, the moment the righteousness of God was heard as a righteousness God gives rather than one he merely demands (McGrath 2005). The Latin tag the Reformers used, sola fide, by faith alone, is just the name for the relief of a man who has finally stopped climbing.

## Granting the Catholic Objection Its Weight

> They burn over a question, and the question underneath the Reformation is the same one still keeping you awake at night.

Steel-man the Catholic objection, because it is serious and the Reformers were not simply right about everything. The split fractured the visible church that Christ prayed would be one. Sola scriptura, the Bible as final authority, did not produce one pure church but thousands of competing ones, each certain it had the plain reading. The Council of Trent's worry, that faith spoken of apart from transformation curdles into a license to sin, was not foolish. The Catholic historian Brad Gregory argues that the Reformation unintentionally fathered the fragmented, secularized, hyper-individual modern world, the world in which, once the final authority has been relocated into each believer's own reading, every person becomes in effect his own interpreter with no court above him (Gregory 2012). Give all of that its full weight. The downstream costs were real, and the Reformers did not foresee them.

And steel-man the secular reduction too, the account that says it was never really about theology. Yes, the printing press spread Luther's tracts faster than Rome could answer them. Yes, German princes had political and financial reasons to shield him from the emperor. Yes, nationalism and money were in the mix. The material factors were genuine. But they explain the speed of the fire, not the fire itself. Erasmus mocked the church's corruption more wittily than Luther ever did and started no reformation, because mockery of corruption is not a gospel. Luther had a gospel.

## The Courtroom the Modern Self Relocated

Now the reversal, the thing the modern reader assumes is behind us. People treat the Reformation as a five-hundred-year-old institutional quarrel the secular world has happily outgrown. It is the reverse. The question it raised is more alive now than it has ever been, because the modern self simply relocated the courtroom. You may no longer fear standing before God, but you stand every single day before some other tribunal, the market, the feed, the mirror, the endless audit of whether you are successful enough, attractive enough, productive enough, enough. Luther's anguish was not a medieval relic. It was the human condition, and the secular age did not cure it. It only removed the one verdict that could ever have silenced it. The performance treadmill is works-righteousness with God deleted, all of the judgment and none of the grace.

## A Pastor Still on the Treadmill

> The performance treadmill is works-righteousness with God deleted, all of the judgment and none of the grace.

I am a Protestant pastor. I preach justification by faith, and I still live half my life on that treadmill, auditing my worth by the size of the crowd and the warmth of the reviews, which means I have heard Luther's discovery and not yet believed it all the way to the floor. The Reformation is not a date I celebrate once a year. It is a deliverance I need again every week.

## Free, Not Merely Brave

> The Reformation is not a date I celebrate once a year. It is a deliverance I need again every week.

Luther stood before the emperor at Worms in 1521 and was ordered to take it all back, and he answered that he could not, because his conscience was captive to the word of God. We remember the courage and forget the relief underneath it. He was not mainly being brave. He was being free, free the way only a man can be who has stopped trying to earn what he has finally learned is given. That freedom is still on offer, and the question that drove him to it is still the only question that finally matters about your life. Not whether you are enough. Whether you will receive the righteousness you could never manufacture. The Reformation was the rediscovery that the answer is yes, and that it costs you nothing, because it already cost God everything.

### Works Cited

Gregory, Brad S. 2012. The Unintended Reformation. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

McGrath, Alister E. 2005. Iustitia Dei: A History of the Christian Doctrine of Justification. 3rd ed. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Taylor, Charles. 2007. A Secular Age. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.

title: The Great Awakenings and the Making of American Faith
excerpt: American Christianity was born in revival. That fire gave it a faith of the heart, and it also taught it to trust feeling over the church. We live in both.
body:
American Christianity was born in fire, and the fire left a mark that is both its genius and its wound.

## Two Fires and the Shape They Left

Twice the country was swept by mass revival, and both times it changed not only how many Americans believed but what believing was. The First Great Awakening broke out in the 1730s and 1740s, when Jonathan Edwards preached and a young Anglican named George Whitefield crossed the colonies drawing crowds of thousands in open fields, and people wept and collapsed and were converted where they stood. The Second came around the turn of the next century, the camp meetings on the frontier, Cane Ridge in Kentucky in 1801 where thousands gathered for days, and the revivalism of Charles Finney, who taught that a revival was not a miracle to be awaited but a result a preacher could produce with the right methods. Out of these two fires came the recognizable shape of American faith. Personal. Emotional. Built on a datable conversion, a moment you were born again.

## The Strongest Case for the Revivals

Take the strongest case for the revivals, because there is a real one. The conversions were often genuine and lasting, and the awakened faith poured itself into reform. The Second Great Awakening fueled the abolitionist movement, the founding of colleges, the care of the poor, the missionary surge that carried the gospel around the world. A faith of the heart rather than a merely inherited and formal religion is exactly what Edwards was defending, and Scripture is on his side, since the first commandment is to love God with all your heart. Pentecost itself, in the second chapter of Acts, was a public outpouring that looked like drunken chaos to the onlookers before it looked like God.

## Edwards and the Test of True Affection

> Heat is not light. A strong feeling is not the Holy Spirit.

But Edwards, the greatest mind the awakenings produced, spent his best book warning that not every flame is the Spirit. In his treatise on the religious affections, in 1746, he set himself the hardest question a revival raises, how to tell true religious feeling from false, and his answer was unflinching. The test of a genuine work of God is not the intensity of the emotion. Tears and trembling and ecstasy can all be counterfeited or self-produced. The test is the fruit, a changed life and a new and lasting love for God and neighbor that remains after the meeting ends (Edwards 1959). Heat is not light. A strong feeling is not the Holy Spirit.

## The Wound of a Democratized Faith

And here the wound shows itself. Nathan Hatch has shown how the awakenings democratized American religion, stripping authority from the educated clergy and the old institutions and handing it to the individual, the itinerant, the common person and his experience (Hatch 1989). This was liberating, and it was corrosive. Finney's new measures treated conversion as a technique to be engineered. The line from there runs straight to revivalism as manipulation, to a deep anti-intellectualism, and to the believer who trusts the warmth in his chest over the creed, the Scripture, and the church. Mark Noll's verdict on the long result is severe, that American evangelicalism, for all its energy, became a movement that never learned to love God with its mind (Noll 1994).

> The buffered modern believer who needs no church and no tradition because he has his own experience of Jesus did not come from secular culture. He came from the revival tent.

Here is the reversal. The thing that looks like America's most distinctive religious genius, the personal experience, the unmediated encounter, the faith you can feel, is also the taproot of its deepest distortion. The buffered modern believer who needs no church and no tradition because he has his own experience of Jesus did not come from secular culture. He came from the revival tent. The awakening that freed the believer from dead formalism also cut him loose from the one community that could ever test whether his feeling was the Spirit or only himself.

## The Feeling I Know How to Manufacture

I preach for conversions, and I want the room to feel something, and I know exactly how to manufacture the feeling, the music under the appeal, the pause, the story, the lowered voice. I have at times mistaken the warmth I produced for the work only God can do. Edwards's question is the one I have to keep asking of my own ministry, and it does not flatter me. Is this fruit, or is it only heat.

## Living in Both Halves of the Inheritance

> Not how hot it burned. What it grew.

The awakenings gave America a faith that could be personally and urgently real, and in a world full of dead religion that is no small gift. They also taught it to trust the fire over the hearth, the moment over the long obedience, the feeling over the body of Christ. We are still living in both halves of that inheritance, and the test Edwards left is still the only way to tell them apart. Not how hot it burned. What it grew.

### Works Cited

Edwards, Jonathan. 1959. A Treatise Concerning Religious Affections. Edited by John E. Smith. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Hatch, Nathan O. 1989. The Democratization of American Christianity. New Haven: Yale University Press.

Noll, Mark A. 1994. The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

title: Why There Are So Many Christian Denominations
excerpt: The thirty-thousand-denominations number is a misused statistic. The real and stubborn fact is how much wildly divided Christians still confess in common.
body:
Someone always brings up the number. There are thirty thousand Protestant denominations, the line goes, so how could anyone possibly know which one is right, and does the chaos not prove the whole thing is just people making it up as they go.

## Being Honest About the Wound

Start by being honest about the wound, because it is real and the New Testament treats it as a scandal. The night before he died, Jesus prayed that his people would be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world would believe (John 17:21). And the first generation was already failing him. In Corinth they were splitting into rival fan clubs, I follow Paul, I follow Apollos, I follow Cephas, and Paul turned on them with a question that should still sting. Is Christ divided (1 Corinthians 1:13 ESV). A fractured church is not a neutral fact. It is a contradiction of the gospel it preaches, and every honest Christian should feel the shame of it.

## The Serious Catholic and Orthodox Critique

Steel-man the Catholic and Orthodox critique, which is the serious one. Protestantism cut the authority of the church loose and put a Bible in every hand, and the predictable result was fragmentation without end, because once every believer is his own final interpreter there is no one left to settle the disputes, and so the body keeps dividing. The visible oneness Christ prayed for is precisely the thing Protestantism seems unable to deliver. That argument has real force, and a Protestant who does not feel its weight is not paying attention.

## A Number Stripped of Its Method

But the famous number is a misuse, and the kind of misuse matters. The thirty thousand figure traces to a particular reference work that counts denominations nation by nation, so that one global communion present in a hundred countries gets counted a hundred times, and that folds in every small independent congregation that ever registered its own name. The source was measuring something other than what the slogan claims. Count actual distinct traditions, the real families of Christian conviction, and the figure is in the dozens, not the tens of thousands. The statistic is not evidence. It is a number stripped of its method and waved like a flag.

## The Center They Have Kept

> A fractured church is not a neutral fact. It is a contradiction of the gospel it preaches, and every honest Christian should feel the shame of it.

Now the reversal, the thing the division cannot hide. Take a Pentecostal in Lagos, a Greek Orthodox in Thessaloniki, a Catholic in Manila, and a Baptist in Alabama, traditions that have argued bitterly for centuries, and put them in one room, and watch how much they still hold in common. They confess the same creed, that God is Father, Son, and Spirit, that Christ was crucified and raised. They baptize. They break bread. They read the same Scriptures and pray to the same Lord. The remarkable thing is not that Christians have disagreed about church government and the mode of baptism. The remarkable thing is that, across two thousand years and every culture on earth and all the blood they have shed, they have kept the same center. Kevin Vanhoozer argues that the Bible in every hand was never bound to fracture the church without end, that a shared reading of the gospel's core can hold a real catholicity together underneath the genuine differences, so that the divisions are not the last word the principle was destined to speak (Vanhoozer 2016). Lesslie Newbigin, who gave his life to Christian unity, insisted that the church is meant to be a sign of the reconciliation God intends for the whole human race, and that its divisions are a wound to be healed, not a reason to abandon the body (Newbigin 1989).

## Scar Tissue, Not Indifference

The denominations, then, are scar tissue. They mark real injuries, genuine disagreements about baptism and authority and the supper, things that mattered enough to fight over because they touched the truth. Pretending the disagreements do not matter is not unity. It is indifference, and indifference is not what Jesus prayed for. He prayed for oneness in the truth, which is harder and costlier than a vague agreement to stop arguing.

> The slogan I follow Paul is alive and well. It has only changed names.

I am a pastor of one particular tradition, and I have at times worn its distinctives like a team jersey, defined more by what I am against than by the Lord I am for, which is the Corinthian disease exactly. The slogan I follow Paul is alive and well. It has only changed names.

## Grieving the Scandal Without Despairing of It

> It is that after everything, underneath all of it, they are still confessing the same crucified and risen Lord.

A divided church is a scandal, and the answer is neither to deny it nor to despair of it. It is to grieve it, to refuse both the cheap unity that pretends truth does not matter and the cheap cynicism that pretends the divisions are the whole story, and to live toward the day Christ prayed for. The number was always a distraction. The real and stubborn fact, the one the skeptic should have to explain, is not that Christians divided. It is that after everything, underneath all of it, they are still confessing the same crucified and risen Lord.

### Works Cited

Newbigin, Lesslie. 1989. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society. Grand Rapids: Eerdmans.

Vanhoozer, Kevin J. 2016. Biblical Authority after Babel. Grand Rapids: Brazos Press.

title: The Crusades: What Actually Happened
excerpt: The Crusades are the favorite club used against the faith. The honest history is worse than the cliche, and its deepest critique is Christian, not secular.
body:
The Crusades are the club. Raise the violence of religion in any argument and they arrive within a sentence, offered as the proof that faith makes people kill. The honest history is worse than the cliche and also more complicated than it, and a Christianity that cannot tell the truth about its own worst chapters has no business asking anyone to trust it about anything.

## Telling the Truth About the Atrocities

So tell the truth. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099, and the soldiers massacred the city, Muslims and Jews together, in a slaughter the chroniclers describe with horror and pride in the same sentence. On the way there, in 1096, crusaders in the Rhineland turned on the Jewish communities and murdered thousands, among the first great pogroms of European history, carried out by men wearing the cross. And the Fourth Crusade, in 1204, never reached a Muslim army at all. It sacked Constantinople, the greatest Christian city in the world, and Christians looted and desecrated the churches of other Christians. None of this can be explained away, and the attempt to explain it away is itself a second offense.

## Granting the Critic His Full Weight

Steel-man the critic fully. The argument made by Christopher Hitchens and Sam Harris is that here is religion doing exactly what religion does, sanctifying slaughter with the name of God, and that the Crusades are not an aberration but a revelation of what belief licenses (Hitchens 2007). Give it its weight. The atrocities were real, they were vast, and they were done explicitly in the name of Christ with the promise of heaven attached. A believer who shrugs that off has not reckoned with it.

## The Cartoon False in the Other Direction

Now the other correction, because the cartoon is false in the opposite direction. The popular picture of the Crusades as unprovoked Western colonial aggression against a peaceful East is bad history. The historians, Thomas Madden and Christopher Tyerman among them, point out that the Crusades came after four centuries of conquest that had taken three-quarters of the formerly Christian world, including the Holy Land itself, and that the First Crusade was called in answer to an appeal from the Christian East against advancing armies (Madden 2005). The medieval crusader was not a modern colonialist. Most went bankrupt going, and many went believing they were defending their brothers and reclaiming stolen ground. The history is a tangle of real grievance and real horror, and both are true at once.

## The Photographic Negative of Its Own Lord

> None of this can be explained away, and the attempt to explain it away is itself a second offense.

But here is the reversal that neither the atheist nor the defensive apologist wants to hear. The Crusades do not indict Christianity by being too Christian. They indict it by being a betrayal of Christianity, the photographic negative of its own Lord. On the night he was arrested, Peter drew a sword to defend him, the one moment in the Gospels a disciple takes up arms for Jesus, and Jesus stopped him cold. Put your sword back into its place, he said, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52 ESV). Standing before Pilate he said that his kingdom was not of this world, and that if it were, his servants would fight (John 18:36). The whole logic of the cross is a king who conquers by dying rather than by killing, who refuses the legions he could have called down. Measure the Crusades against that and they are not the fruit of the faith. They are its inversion.

## The Most Devastating Critique Is the Christian One

> Measure the Crusades against that and they are not the fruit of the faith. They are its inversion.

Which means the most devastating critique of the Crusades is not the atheist's. It is the Christian one. The atheist says religion made them violent. The gospel says they abandoned the religion the moment they raised a sword in its name, because the founder of it went unarmed to his own execution and told his followers the world would know them by their love and not by their conquests. You cannot use the Crusades to refute a faith whose Lord and whose earliest martyrs died precisely by refusing to do what the crusaders did.

## The Crusading Impulse That Never Died

> We did this. Some version of we keeps doing it.

It is easy to condemn men dead a thousand years. The harder thing is to notice that the crusading impulse, the certainty that God's cause can be advanced by force and that our enemies are therefore his, did not die in the Middle Ages. It only traded the sword for other weapons, the culture war waged as though it were a holy war, the opponent to be crushed rather than the neighbor to be loved. We did this. Some version of we keeps doing it.

The church should not flinch from the Crusades, and it should not excuse them. It should own them, and then it should say the one thing that is both true and damning. They were done in the name of a Lord who would have stopped them, who did stop Peter, who chose the cross over the sword and asked his people to do the same. The kingdom of God has never once advanced by killing for him. It has only ever advanced by people willing to die for him. The crusaders forgot which one they were called to. So, often, do we.

### Works Cited

Hitchens, Christopher. 2007. God Is Not Great. New York: Twelve.

Madden, Thomas F. 2005. The New Concise History of the Crusades. Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield.

Tyerman, Christopher. 2006. God's War: A New History of the Crusades. Cambridge, MA: Belknap Press.
